articles.title: Dodgers activate Shohei Ohtani, demote red-hot rookie Josue De Paula to Triple-A
articles.summary: De Paula is reportedly still in the mix for a postseason roster spot.
articles.body:
As expected , the Los Angeles Dodgers activated Shohei Ohtani from the injured list on Wednesday. In a corresponding move, they demoted a player who turned out to be a more capable replacement than anyone could've imagined for two weeks.

That would be rookie slugger Josue De Paula, who was optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City, a team whose season could end as soon as Wednesday. De Paula, the top prospect in the Dodgers' system and one of the best overall prospects in baseball, was promoted to replace Ohtani on the roster .

Ohtani will hit second in his first game back against the San Diego Padres , marking his first time not batting leadoff for the Dodgers since June 16, 2024. The red-hot Mookie Betts is filling the leadoff spot instead against Padres left-hander Robbie Ray .

De Paula, meanwhile, will be making his Triple-A debut as a starter for the Oklahoma City Comets in Game 2 of the PCL championship series.

In the 11 games Ohtani missed, no player on the Dodgers reached base more than De Paula. The Dodgers went 11-3 in that span and clinched both a playoff berth and the NL West while moving into strong position to secure a wild-card bye.

Between his cameo in L.A. and a performance in Double-A that won him Texas League MVP honors at 21 years old, De Paula has inspired questions about a place on the Dodgers' postseason roster.

As The Athletic's Katie Woo points out , De Paula being optioned on Wednesday means he will be eligible to be recalled by Oct. 3, when the Dodgers will begin playing the NLDS. He isn't technically eligible for the playoffs because he wasn't on the Los Angeles 40-man roster on Sept. 1, but that can be remedied by petitioning the commissioner's office for him to replace a player going on the injured list.

With Ohtani taking up the designated hitter spot and corner outfielders Teoscar Hernandez and Kyle Tucker both resurrecting down seasons over the past month or so, there's not a natural place for De Paula in the starting lineup.

Per The Athletic, De Paula is still in the mix for a postseason roster spot but appears to be in competition with Dalton Rushing for the role of premium left-handed bench bat. Rushing has been attempting to play through a partially torn UCL since early August. He won't be playing his usual catcher position again in 2026, but he could still hit.

Rushing is expected to be activated sometime this week, at which point he too will be trying to justify October at-bats in the final games of the regular season. De Paula has set a high bar to clear in that regard.

Figuring out where to put a rising star because your superstar is healthy again is ultimately a good problem to have. Whoever is on the roster, the Dodgers are on track to play the Atlanta Braves or Padres in the NLDS, though that could still change in the coming days.

articles.title: Aaron Judge's latest injury offers a glimpse of a rapidly approaching Yankees future
articles.summary: Entering October without a world-beating Judge is a bizarre new possibility — and also one the Yankees might need to get familiar with.
articles.body:
Their doubleheader split with the Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday ensured that the Bombers will enter the postseason as the top wild card in the American League . (The Rays clinched the AL East and the No. 1 seed ). That means, barring a major surprise over the next few days, New York is set to host its forever rivals , the Boston Red Sox , in a best-of-three series starting Tuesday in the Bronx.

But while the schedule and the opponent offer a dose of certainty, there's one enormous unknown swirling around YankeeLand: the health of three-time MVP Aaron Judge .

It has been an injury-riddled season for the Yankees' captain, who missed more than three months due to a stress fracture on his first rib. He returned Sept. 8 and appeared in seven games, tallying four hits and one homer, before landing back on the shelf due to a calf strain suffered Sept. 16. Predictably, the Yankees have been quite mum about Judge's status. Skipper Aaron Boone first declined to disclose the severity of the strain but eventually described it as "moderate."

Before Tuesday's doubleheader, Boone told reporters that Judge won't return during the regular season and that the Yankees are "planning on him not being a part" of the team's wild-card exploits. On Wednesday, Judge reversed course, telling reporters that he intends to be ready for wild-card Game 1 . So while the door remains open on a heroic comeback from the goliath slugger, the possibility of Judge taking in October's opening act from the dugout still looms large.

In the event that he does return next week, it's difficult to envision Judge doing so at full strength. Notably, the calf issue is on his right leg — his rear or plant leg. Judge's swing mechanics are particularly reliant on his having explosiveness and stability in his right hip and right leg. Without that, he could be a shell of his best self. Still, players are famously more willing to use certain medications and numbing agents in the postseason, things that could help push Judge onto the roster.

His not being able to play in the outfield is another consideration. Even after the lengthy layoff, Judge slotted immediately back into right field, in part because the Yankees' roster is overloaded with designated hitter types. A more cautious course of action might've saved Judge's calf from giving out, though it's impossible to know for sure.

But now, given the glut of DHs on New York 's roster, it's hard to imagine a super-reduced version of Judge being the optimal choice in the lineup over Ben Rice or Paul Goldschmidt . As such, how Boone slots Judge back into the mix if he's able to play will be one of the more fascinating storylines to follow.

Otherwise, the Yanks might need to soldier on, a man — one very large man — down.

This era of Yankees baseball has simultaneously been shaped by Judge and shaped around him. Critics have argued the current roster is overly dependent on the future Hall of Famer — a ridiculous proposition. Wouldn't anyone build a team around one of the world's best hitters? Still, entering October without a world-beating Judge is a bizarre new possibility and, at the same time, one the Yankees, given Judge's age, might need to acquaint themselves with.

New York has not played a postseason contest without Judge since the 2015 winner-take-all wild-card game. A 40-year-old Alex Rodriguez hit fourth for the Yanks that day. Dallas Keuchel threw six shutout innings for a plucky, likable Houston Astros team yet to villainize themselves in the baseball world. Colby Rasmus and Carlos Gómez each ripped solo homers in Houston's victory. Since then, Judge has appeared in all 65 of New York's playoff games, the most over that span by a non-Dodger or non-Astro.

Of course, Judge's physical woes this season do not necessarily portend the beginning of the end. Playing through pain and in a small sample, the 6-foot-7 Californian still posted an impressive .871 OPS. He was, less than a year ago, the American League MVP. He surely has more magical moments to conjure, more souvenirs to crank into the seats. And yet, the clock is undeniably ticking. Father Time, you see, has never been defeated.

The Yankees' captain will turn 35 in April. There have been only 22 individual MLB seasons since integration (1947) in which a qualified player 35 or older finished with an OPS over 1.000. Seven of those years — five from Barry Bonds, one from Mark McGwire and one from Manny Ramírez — were likely aided by performance enhancers. The list, understandably, grows only smaller as the age ticks closer to 40. It's hard to be elite; it's even harder as your body decays.

Judge could certainly ward off Father Time and his sinister ways and remain otherworldly for a few more years. Ted Williams did it. So did Henry Aaron and Chipper Jones and David Ortiz . Some folks age like fine wine. Judge is disciplined, driven and athletic enough to make it work. Modern medical and training technology make it easier for the best to stay healthy for longer. Nobody would be shocked if Judge has another MVP season in him.

But the opposite is also true. Even if his production doesn't tumble off a cliff, there's reason to be wary about the future. Judge cannot carry this franchise around on his broad shoulders forever. Eventually, the Yankees will need to pivot, grow, change, chart a new course. And given the club's institutional smarts and financial might, chances are they'll find another aircraft carrier on which to center the franchise.

Besides, the Yankees' pitching-driven success this year is a reminder that such a path is possible, even fruitful. The 2026 New York Yankees have won a lot of games without Judge. They might need to continue doing so in October.

articles.title: Aaron Judge says he plans to be ready for Yankees' wild-card series, disputing comments from manager Aaron Boone
articles.summary: The Yankees' star has been out since Saturday due to a calf strain.
articles.body:
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Tuesday that franchise star Aaron Judge will not play in the team's wild-card series next week . Judge himself had a different story a day later.

The three-time AL MVP told ESPN that he intends to be ready for Game 1 of the wild-card series on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium.

"That's what the plan is," Judge said. "Try to get my body ready so I'm ready to go."

Judge has been on the injured list since Saturday due to a right calf strain , the latest blow in the worst season of his career. He reportedly received a platelet-poor plasma injection in the knee on Monday and is waiting for clearance to resume activity with his injured leg.

The Yankees can technically activate Judge on the final day of the regular season, but his potential return date is unclear. While addressing Judge's health with reporters, Boone said, "We're planning on him not being a part of that," seemingly ruling Judge out until at least the ALDS if the Yankees advance.

Judge reportedly said he has had discussions with the Yankees' decision-makers about his prognosis, but he doesn't know if he will be on the club's wild-card roster:

"We've done a lot of talks, but I can't control what people say," Judge said. "So you'll have to talk to them about that."

If the season ended Wednesday, the Yankees would face the Boston Red Sox in the wild-card series for a second straight season. They have already clinched the top wild-card spot in the AL, with the Red Sox three games ahead of the Chicago White Sox for the second spot.

A healthy Judge would be a boon to the Yankees, but there's no telling what they will get from him even if he's on the roster. This season has been a trying one for the 34-year-old, who has played only 66 games due to that calf injury and a stress fracture in his ribs. That's the fewest games he has played in a season outside of his cup of coffee in 2016 and the COVID-shortened 2020 season.

Judge has also underperformed even when playing, slashing .241/.360/.511 with a 141 OPS+ that ranks, again, as the worst of his career outside of 2016.

articles.title: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. Drops Viral Quote on 2026 Slump After Signing $500M Blue Jays Contract
articles.summary: It has largely been a season to forget for Vladimir Guerrero Jr. from an individual standpoint, which made his recent comments about the 14-year, $500 million contract he and the Toronto Blue Jays agreed to in April 2025 all the more notable.
articles.body:
It has largely been a season to forget for Vladimir Guerrero Jr. from an individual standpoint, which made his recent comments about the 14-year, $500 million contract he and the Toronto Blue Jays agreed to in April 2025 all the more notable.

As Mitch Bannon of The Athletic noted, comments the slugger made on a Spanish-language interview with Dominican broadcaster Victoria Batista suggested players are paid for their past accomplishments and not as much for what will happen over the course of a new deal.

"I don't regret myself," Guerrero said through an interpreter after the comments circulated on social media. "I'm not lying, what I'm saying. I understand some fans, they don't understand the way or what I was trying to say, specifically. But what I said was the way I feel."

Ranking MLB's 10 Greatest Postseason Runs Since 2000 🏆

Guerrero was one of the best players in the league prior to his new contract.

From 2021 through 2025, he was an All-Star five straight years, a Silver Slugger twice, a Gold Glover once and finished in the top 10 of American League MVP voting twice. That included in 2021 when he finished second in MVP voting.

He led the league in home runs (48), on-base percentage (.401), slugging percentage (.601), OPS (1.002) and runs scored (123) that year and seemed well on his way to a Hall of Fame career seeing how it was his age-22 season.

Even last year, he led the Blue Jays to the World Series with eight home runs in 18 playoff games.

Yet it has been a different story in 2026 with a .263/.336/.359 slash line, nine home runs and 56 RBI in 141 games. The numbers are a far cry from when he was at his best and one reason the Blue Jays did not make the AL playoffs.

"Obviously I feel really bad about the year I had," Guerrero said. "I couldn't get my team to the postseason."

Fortunately for the Blue Jays, Guerrero is just 27 years old. It is not unrealistic to expect him to return to form next year and beyond, which would make the 2026 campaign more of an anomaly than anything else.

While his past performance surely played a significant role in the contract negotiations with Toronto, the team likely also assumed his level of production would remain steady during at least the first part of that deal.

If that is going to be the case, he will have to quickly put the 2026 campaign in the rearview mirror.

articles.body: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has four games left before he can put his 2026 Toronto Blue Jays season behind him. Guerrero, the six-time All-Star who signed the third highest-paid extension in MLB history in April 2025 at $500 million, has hit just nine home runs and slugged .359 to date for a career-low .695 OPS to date. "I understand why the fans believe it’s the other way around. Sometimes, I think that way, too, like, ‘Oh, they give me this money, and I’m not doing enough,’ but you know I try my best, and I’m working hard. "The fans, I know how they are, when you are doing great they are 100% behind you. But when you are not at your best, not everybody is behind you, almost nobody supports you. Those are my real fans, the ones that are supporting me all the time." After catching heat from Blue Jays fans, Guerrero was approached about the viral quotes, which he responded to. Then, the kind of playoffs that I had to help the team get into the World Series. "To the fans, I’ve never stopped working very hard. I am going to go into the offseason again to prepare myself the best I can. Physically, mentally, everything that I have like I always do for my team and my teammates." In Guerrero’s defense, that is technically what the Blue Jays did when they dished out his 14-year, $500 million extension, which is only behind Shohei Ohtani’s 10-year, $700 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Juan Soto’s 15-year, $765 million deal with the New York Mets. The franchise paid Guerrero for what he did from his debut in 2019 up to a fantastic 2025 campaign, where he belted eight homers and hit .397 across 18 postseason games. But these comments show that Guerrero mustn’t be aware of what putting pen to money-filled paper meant in April 2025. No longer is it time in any sport, let alone Major League Baseball, where contracts are dished out based solely on past performance. It’s looking ahead to the future, where those past performances are expected to continue through a much-more lucrative deal. MLB franchises sign players to contracts based on the market, and that market is justified by how the player will perform for them later on, while obviously looking at the track record in the past. With any investment, those dishing out the big bucks want a return. So, in a season where the home run total for a slugger is less than double digits – he still has time to at least get to 10 – and a career-low WAR (albeit the 2020 COVID-shortened campaign) has been accumulated, the Blue Jays and its fan base have every right to be disappointed. Yes, Guerrero was a major reason why Toronto reached the World Series in 2025, but the team and its fans are also allowed to voice displeasure with not just a down year – a career-worst performance in various metrics. Would the Mets have dished out the highest-paying contract in league history if they didn’t expect Soto to continue performing at his superstar pace? articles.title: Giancarlo Stanton Injury Update, Status for MLB Playoffs Given by Yankees' Boone Ahead of Wild Card
articles.summary: New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone provided an update on Giancarlo Stanton's health heading into the 2026 postseason.
articles.body:
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone provided an update on Giancarlo Stanton's health heading into the 2026 postseason.

Boone said Wednesday that he was putting Stanton "on the outskirts of the conversation" regarding the playoffs, per the Associated Press (h/t ESPN ).

The 36-year-old faced pitchers and ran the bases at Double-A Somerset on Wednesday as he continues to recover from calf issues. If Stanton is able to return during the postseason, he's expected to operate in a reduced role.

"You're looking more at a pinch-hit scenario," Boone said about Stanton, via ESPN. "We'll see if that's even a realistic option."

Stanton hasn't appeared in a game since April 24, as he initially suffered a calf strain before experiencing multiple setbacks as he attempted to work his way back into New York's lineup.

The five-time All-Star has suited up in just 24 contests this season, hitting .256 with three home runs and 14 RBI.

Stanton has been limited by injuries in recent years, appearing in just 292 of a possible 486 games from 2023-25.

Still, it isn't hard to imagine him providing a boost to the Yankees' offense if he can return.

Despite Stanton's health woes, he's been a consistent contributor for the Bronx Bombers throughout their postseason runs. He owns a .926 OPS in his playoff career, racking up 18 homers in 48 games.

The Yankees are locked into an American League Wild Card spot after the Tampa Bay Rays clinched the AL East on Tuesday.

Game 1 of New York's AL Wild Card series is on Sept. 29.

articles.title: Rangers' failure spells end of not only 2026, but of this era of baseball in Arlington
articles.summary: Texas' three-game losing streak this week just about snuffs out any remaining flicker of hope for this season and big changes loom in the offseason.
articles.body:
ARLINGTON — The story of the Texas Rangers ' season: In the season's biggest moment, when the Rangers really needed a World Series hero to come through, one did. It just wasn't any of the ones they kept.

Marcus Semien trotted around the bases on Wednesday. Hit a go-ahead homer.

The guys from the 2023 World Series team that still wear the Rangers' colors? Oh, they were a combined 1 for 15 in a 7-2 loss to the Mets that just about snuffs the last flicker of hope from the Rangers season .

"We haven't produced enough to win," manager Skip Schumaker said after a third consecutive loss in which the Rangers have scored a total of seven runs. "We had to win games. These are must-win games. That's just the reality of it.

"There is definitely frustration. You can sense it in the dugout. You can feel it. They know they are better than they've shown the last couple of nights."

About that, let us offer an alternative: Maybe they are not.

Also, if you think the Rangers are frustrated, just consider how Chris Young feels.

Which brings us to a point. Not only are the lights on the season about to go out, but also up in smoke is this era of Rangers baseball, whatever this era was or is. Should've been the Golden Era. It does, after all, include a World Series trophy. Then again, with another loss, the Rangers will have nine non-winning seasons in the last 10. Only thing Golden these days at the ballpark is the occasional rendition of the Huntrix single, blared at levels that can break the average noise dosimeter.

The offense hasn't gotten significantly better. We're talking about three straight years, multiple hitting coaches and managers. The Rangers tried patience in 2024. Didn't work. Made a bunch of changes the next winter. Nope. This year, the OPS has shown improvement, mostly due to higher walk rates. But the runs per game is actually down from last year.

At the center of any conversation over next year's offense will be how the Rangers proceed with Corey Seager , who struggled, was hurt, came back strong and has disappeared at the most critical moment of the season. His OPS (.732) is 2% higher than league average. In the Rangers' three-game losing streak, he's 0 for 15 with five strikeouts and has gone hitless in his last six at-bats with runners in scoring position.

"Obviously not as productive as you'd like to be right now, yeah," Seager said when asked about the frustration of the current slump. "You'd like to be better down the stretch in these important games, but you just have to come back tomorrow and keep plugging."

Seager's going to be 33 next year. He's missed almost 200 games over the last four seasons. He's got five years left on his contract. The Rangers are going to have to have a long talk about his future.

But he's not the only one. Where does Evan Carter , once the "Little Savior," fit in? He's unplayable against lefties and has a .600 OPS for the season. On Wednesday, with the bases loaded against Nolan McLean , with a walk to be offered, he swung at two pitches out of the zone and grounded into a fielder's choice. Two innings later, he deadened a ball nicely for what would have been a solid sac bunt, but was instead his attempt at bunting for a hit.

And it doesn't stop there. Wyatt Langford is 1 for 10 in the losing streak with six strikeouts. He's hitting .237 now in his third full season in the majors. His OPS is down 15 points from last year. It's a Nomar Mazara-esque fade. By that we mean, getting worse at a point where he should be hitting his prime.

This was supposed to be a huge part of the Rangers' core. They have come up short at the most important moment of the season and, quite frankly, for much of the earlier part, too.

So c'mon out for the regular season home finale and take a look at the guys. A lot is likely to change the next time you see the Rangers.

articles.title: 1 Stat That Defines Every MLB Team's 2026 Season
articles.summary: No sport has a deeper well of available statistics than baseball. That provides a unique opportunity to tell the story of a team's entire season with one piece of statistical evidence in a way that might not be possible in other sports.
articles.body:
No sport has a deeper well of available statistics than baseball. That provides a unique opportunity to tell the story of a team's entire season with one piece of statistical evidence in a way that might not be possible in other sports.

That's exactly what we set out to do here. The range of statistical analysis covers everything from individual performance to season-long trends to one hot or cold streak that ultimately reshaped a club's entire 2026 trajectory.

As the regular season winds down, let's sum up the 2026 campaign of all 30 MLB teams with one defining stat.

The Stat: 162 days since they were last above .500

After a busy offseason of retooling the pitching staff and signing Pete Alonso, the Orioles entered the season hoping to rebound from a disappointing 2025. They went 9-7 over their first 16 games to hold a share of the AL East lead, but they lost their next two games. April 14 now stands as the last day they were above the .500 mark this year.

The Stat: 15.6 WAR combined from four marquee offseason additions

The Red Sox absolutely nailed their offseason, adding Sonny Gray (28 GS, 2.82 ERA, 163.0 IP, 4.0 WAR) and Ranger Suarez (27 GS, 3.27 ERA, 143.1 IP, 2.5 WAR) to the rotation, while Willson Contreras (154 OPS+, 27 HR, 4.6 WAR) and Caleb Durbin (105 OPS+, 39 XBH, 20 SB, 4.5 WAR) were brought aboard to stabilize the infield. Without the contributions of those four players, this might not be a playoff team.

The last time Aaron Judge missed significant time in 2023, the Yankees went 57-49 (.538) with him in the lineup, compared to 25-31 (.446) without him. They finished 82-80 and missed the postseason. This year's group has no doubt missed having his superstar bat in the middle of the lineup, but they have done a far better job weathering the storm of his absence.

After spending the 2025 season transplanted to Steinbrenner Field while repairs were made to Tropicana Field, the Rays have returned home this year in dominant fashion. Their 55-26 home record is the best in baseball. Those 55 wins also represent the most in a single season at The Trop. Clinching the best record in the AL on Tuesday could be huge for their October outlook.

The Stat: 11th in HR in 2025 (191), 28th in HR in 2026 (149)

The Blue Jays had one of the most potent offenses in baseball a year ago, especially in October when they slugged 28 home runs in 18 games and posted an .823 OPS as a team en route to the World Series. This year, that power production has dried up in shocking fashion, as their 149 home runs are tied for last in the majors. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has just nine long balls in 596 plate appearances. He didn't hit his first home run at the Rogers Centre until Sept. 13.

The Stat: 74 consecutive days in first place before Sept. 16 loss

The White Sox's resurgence was one of the biggest storylines of the season for months while they sat atop the AL Central, but a 5-12 stretch in late August and early September culminated in surrendering their division lead following a loss to the Guardians on Sept. 16. They are still in the projected playoff picture, but the late collapse is threatening to overtake the return to relevance as the story of the season.

The Stat: 12.1 WAR from Parker Messick, Chase DeLauter and Travis Bazzana

Cheap, controllable homegrown talent is the lifeblood of the Cleveland organization, given their preference to steer clear of high-priced free-agent signings or blockbuster trades. That makes the performance of the rookie trio of Parker Messick (31 GS, 2.55 ERA, 183.1 IP, 6.2 WAR), Chase DeLauter (133 OPS+, 47 XBH, 3.5 WAR) and Travis Bazzana (110 OPS+, 37 XBH, 2.4 WAR) one of the biggest reasons they are battling for a division title.

Remove a disastrous month of May and the Tigers have gone 68-62 the rest of the season. That is good for a .523 winning percentage. To put that into perspective, the Guardians currently sit atop the AL Central standings with a .522 winning percentage. One brutal month that included eight straight series losses was enough to completely derail Detroit's entire season.

The Stat: 6.5 WAR for Bobby Witt Jr., 20.0 WAR for 52 other Royals players

The Royals have a true superstar and face of the franchise in Bobby Witt Jr., but there is simply not enough impact talent around him for the team to be competitive, even in the wide-open AL Central. He has accounted for 24.5 percent of the team's overall WAR this year. If you add Michael Wacha (4.3) to the equation, those two represent more than 40 percent of the total tally.

The Stat: 7-4 record immediately before the trade deadline

It might sound like an insignificant 11-game stretch in the grand scheme of things, but it was enough to convince the Twins to pivot away from selling Ryan Jeffers and others at the deadline. Instead, they added Jeff Hoffman, A.J. Minter and Dean Kremer. They are 18-27 since the trade deadline, battling for third place in the AL Central standings rather than a playoff spot.

The Stat: 437 total games played by their Opening Day Nos. 1-5 hitters

On paper, it looked like the Athletics might quietly have one of the best offenses in baseball in 2026, with an outside shot at wild-card contention if the pitching staff could pull its weight. Instead, Nick Kurtz (99 G), Shea Langeliers (101 G), Tyler Soderstrom (109 G), Brent Rooker (48 G) and Jacob Wilson (80 G) have all missed significant time. They have tumbled from 12th to 21st in the majors in runs scored.

The Stat: .232/.298/.389 slash line from Astros hitters other than Yordan Alvarez

Yordan Alvarez is challenging for the AL Triple Crown, hitting .314 with 41 home runs and 102 RBI. He is the heavy favorite for AL MVP honors even as the Astros fight for their playoff lives. One of the biggest reasons they are still on the bubble, hovering around the .500 mark, is the complete lack of offensive consistency around Alvarez. A 687 OPS from the rest of the team tells the story.

The Stat: .382 winning percentage, worst in franchise history

The Angels will finish with a losing record for the 11th consecutive season, so the fact that this year's team is on track to finish with the worst winning percentage in franchise history perfectly illustrates how little progress has been made in righting the ship in more than a decade of futility. They need to go 4-1 over their last five games to finish ahead of the 2024 team that finished 63-99.

The Mariners finished 10th in OPS last season when they came one win away from reaching the World Series. With Cal Raleigh, Julio Rodríguez, Randy Arozarena and a full season of Josh Naylor and newcomer Brendan Donovan, the offense looked even better entering the 2026 season. Instead, Raleigh and Naylor have both regressed. Rodríguez is having the worst season of his career, while Donovan has played 39 games.

The Stat: 67.7% save percentage, 9th in MLB

If there was one weakness to circle on the Rangers roster entering the season, it was the bullpen, which had a glaring lack of proven late-inning options anchoring the relief corps. Thanks in large part to an All-Star campaign from starter-turned-reliever Jacob Latz (56 G, 30/34 SV, 2.08 ERA), nailing down victories has actually been a strength, while Jakob Junis and Tyler Alexander have been rock-solid in setup roles.

The Stat: 3.76 SP ERA, 6th in MLB / 3rd in NL

With Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all on the injured list at the start of the year, a lack of consistent starting pitching behind ace Chris Sale looked like it would derail the 2026 Braves. Instead, they have one of the best rotations in baseball, with Grant Holmes (29 GS, 3.47 ERA, 147.2 IP), Martín Pérez (26 GS, 3.04 ERA, 142.0 IP) and deadline pickup Tyler Mahle (8 GS, 1.28 ERA, 49.1 IP) stepping up big.

The Stat: 20-6 record in June, 21-33 in May and July

A 77-80 record has been enough for the Marlins to hang around on the fringe of contention for much of the year, but a fantastic June has largely propped up their season. While the Detroit Tigers' season imploded with an ugly May, the Marlins have looked more competitive than they actually are throughout the second half, thanks to that 20-6 performance in June.

The Stat: -0.6 combined WAR from six marquee offseason additions

The Mets added Bo Bichette, Marcus Semien, Jorge Polanco, Luis Robert Jr., Freddy Peralta and Devin Williams to the roster during the offseason in their latest attempt to throw money at the problem. That group has combined for negative-0.6 WAR. It's not one bad performance dragging the group down. Bichette is the "leader" with 0.7 WAR while pulling in a $42 million salary.

The Stat: 5.8 WAR from hitters (30th in MLB), 29.7 WAR from pitchers (1st in MLB)

Outside of Bryce Harper (132 OPS+, 3.2 WAR) and Kyle Schwarber (128 OPS+, 2.7 WAR), no other Phillies regular has a WAR higher than 1.2 or an OPS+ higher than 91. Meanwhile, Cristopher Sanchez (7.7 WAR), Jesus Luzardo (6.4 WAR) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR) all rank among the top 10 starters in WAR, while Aaron Nola (3.2 WAR) and Jhoan Duran (3.2 WAR) are also having strong seasons. Can pitching carry them in October?

The Stat: 803 runs scored (3rd in MLB), 796 runs allowed (27th in MLB)

Led by 30-homer seasons from James Wood and CJ Abrams, along with the quietly excellent Daylen Lile, the Nationals have had one of baseball's highest scoring offenses all season. However, they have not had the pitching to match, especially in the bullpen where their 42 blown saves are 10 more than any other team.

The Stat: No. 1 offense, No. 1 defense, No. 29 pitching staff

According to FanGraphs, the Cubs lead the majors in position-player WAR (37.0), the all-encompassing offensive value metric Off (113.6) and the defensive equivalent Def (48.1). However, they are all the way down at 29th in pitcher WAR (5.4), ahead of only the Nationals (5.2). They have managed to navigate those shortcomings on the mound during the regular season, but the lights tend to shine brighter on pitching issues in October.

The Stat: .218 AVG with RISP, worst in MLB

The Reds' .218 average with runners in scoring position is not only the worst in the majors, but it's miles behind the Angels (.234) and Mariners (.233), who rank 28th and 29th in that category. The arc of their season shifted during an eight-game losing streak at the beginning of May, but a season-long struggle to deliver in the clutch is why they have been unable to get the train back on the tracks.

The Stat: 82-45 record since May 1, best in MLB

The Brewers were completely ordinary at 16-14 through their first 30 games, putting them in fourth place in the NL Central standings entering May. Since then, they have been the best team in baseball, logging a .646 winning percentage that would translate to 105 wins over a full season. Even with the slow start, their 98 wins are already a franchise record.

The Stat: 30th to 5th in runs scored, 7th to 17th in ERA

The Pirates set out to overhaul the league's worst offense this past offseason, with Brandon Lowe and Ryan O'Hearn among their notable additions, alongside the impending arrival of uber-prospect Konnor Griffin. The offensive turnaround has been a glowing success, but the pitching staff that was supposed to be the foundation of what they are building has regressed significantly, capping them at a modest improvement over last year's 71-91 finish.

The Stat: 17.2 WAR from young offensive core

The Cardinals exceeded expectations for several months, but 2026 still ultimately served as a rebuilding year. The biggest positive takeaway has been the formation of a legitimate offensive core. Jordan Walker (127 OPS+, 28 HR, 100 RBI, 3.5 WAR) and Alec Burleson (130 OPS+, 23 HR, 111 RBI) have been a dynamic one-two punch in the middle of the lineup. The middle infield tandem of JJ Wetherholt (4.6 WAR) and Masyn Winn (2.8 WAR) has been rock solid, while Iván Herrera (3.0 WAR) earned his first All-Star selection.

The Stat: 83 wins, more than every AL Central and AL West team, 7th in NL

It's a great year to be an AL team on the wild-card bubble, as the 81-win White Sox currently hold the No. 3 spot in the standings, while the 78-win Rangers are also still alive. The D-backs have more wins than every AL Central and AL West team right now, but are staring up at a four-game deficit in the wild-card race and likely watching the postseason from home.

The Stat: 5th team in MLB history with four straight 100-loss seasons

Only five times in MLB history has a team lost 100 games in four consecutive seasons. The last time it happened was the 1962-65 Mets. They were in their first four years as an expansion team. The Rockies seem perfectly content to let the futility wash over them, with no real push to rebuild or retool, even though they haven't won a playoff game since 2009.

The Stat: 14 different starting pitchers, NL-best 3.46 SP ERA

In an ideal world, the Dodgers would get more than a combined 34 starts and 192 innings out of Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Shohei Ohtani, but that hasn't stopped them from posting the best starters' ERA in the NL. They faced a Padres team fighting for playoff position with ace Michael King on the mound on Tuesday and blanked them 7-0 behind a Brock Stewart-led bullpen game that featured eight different pitchers.

Last season, the Guardians were the team that got hot when it mattered most, using a 20-7 record in September to erase a 10.5-game deficit in the AL Central standings and win the division. The Padres are not going to overtake the Dodgers, but they were neck and neck with the D-backs for the No. 3 wild-card spot entering the season's final month. They are now vying for a chance to play host in the Wild Card Round.

The Stat: 0/10 Opening Day starters currently on the active roster

Here's the Giants' Opening Day lineup, and where they are now:

2B Luis Arraez — traded to PHI 3B Matt Chapman — 60-day IL since Aug. 11 DH Rafael Devers — 60-day IL since Sept. 15 SS Willy Adames — 10-day IL since Aug. 23 RF Jung Hoo Lee — 10-day IL since Sept. 20 LF Heliot Ramos — traded to NYY 1B Casey Schmitt — 60-day IL since July 27 C Patrick Bailey — traded to CLE CF Harrison Bader — 60-day IL since May 29 SP Logan Webb — 15-day IL since Sept. 13

That's how a season that began with some legitimate optimism devolves into a 93-loss disaster.

articles.title: 2026 MLB Awards Picks For AL and NL MVP, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, Every Major Award
articles.summary: We'll have to wait until mid-November to officially find out who wins Major League Baseball's Most Valuable Player, Cy Young and Rookie of the Year awards for 2026.
articles.body:
We'll have to wait until mid-November to officially find out who wins Major League Baseball's Most Valuable Player, Cy Young and Rookie of the Year awards for 2026.

But if you're not that patient, we can go ahead and unofficially declare those winners now.

For the most part, this year's awards races have been pretty boring. Shohei Ohtani vs. Pete Crow-Armstrong for NL MVP was a fun debate for about a week, but PCA is probably going to win unanimously at this point. That might also be true for AL MVP, both Cy Youngs and maybe even both Rookies of the Year.

At any rate, there's nothing even remotely close to last year's Aaron Judge vs. Cal Raleigh debate.

For each of those six awards, though, who is most likely to finish as first runner-up? Who has slipped through the cracks and not gotten nearly as much attention as they deserve?

Before we get into those big six, we'll start with a few much more debatable awards, like Manager and Comeback Player of the Year.

Statistics current through the start of play on Wednesday.

AL CPOY : Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

MLB has been officially naming a comeback player of the year in each league on an annual basis since 2005. The only player thus far to win both this award and MVP in the same season was Buster Posey in 2012. Alvarez is destined for both trophies after playing in just 48 games with a sub-.800 OPS in 2025. Not only has he bounced back, but he has been better than ever before.

Also Worth Considering: Shane McClanahan, Gerrit Cole, Mike Trout, Willson Contreras, Nick Martinez

NL CPOY : Sandy Alcantara, Miami Marlins

Of all the awards we'll get into today, this one is the toughest to pick.

Zack Wheeler deserves serious consideration for a dominant return from thoracic outlet syndrome surgery. However, because he merely missed the final six weeks of last season and the first four weeks of the current campaign, he might get overlooked.

Eduardo Rodriguez was dreadful over the past two seasons, posting an ERA north of 5.00 in each, but he is under 3.00 this season and is the biggest reason the Diamondbacks have made it this far with a postseason pulse.

Michael Harris II has also had a major bounce back from a disappointing 2025.

If you possibly had Ty France penciled in as San Diego's best hitter in 2026 after four separate teams in the previous two years sent him packing with a sub-.700 OPS, please step forward to claim your prize.

Alcantara probably takes the cake for returning to his throne as the rubber-armed ace of the Marlins. He missed all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery and had a horrendous first four months of last season. He returned to his old self this year, leading the majors in innings pitched with a sub-4.00 ERA.

Also Considered: Zack Wheeler, Eduardo Rodriguez, Ty France, Michael Harris II, Nolan Arenado, Garrett Mitchell, Tanner Scott

AL Reliever of the Year : Louis Varland, Toronto Blue Jays

It was clear from last October that the Blue Jays had a lot of faith in Varland, using him in a record-setting 15 postseason games. He did so with a 3.94 ERA. He entered 2026 with a career 4.66 ERA during the regular season and nary a save in his big-league career.

This year, though, he was pretty much forced into the closer role in late April by Jeff Hoffman's struggles and subsequently became the king of the ninth inning, going 34-for-36 in save chances with a 1.29 ERA in 77 innings pitched.

Also Worth Considering: Cade Smith, Bryan Baker, Paul Blackburn, Jacob Latz

NL Reliever of the Year : Mason Miller, San Diego Padres

Varland winning the AL award would have been unthinkable six months ago, but Miller doing so in the NL was the expectation all along.

Miller was special from the outset with the Athletics, but getting traded to the Padres last summer unlocked a whole new level of dominance. Between his 85 regular season and two postseason appearances with San Diego, he has a 1.06 ERA, a 0.78 WHIP and a 17.0 K/9.

He has gone 37-for-40 in save chances this season, with two of the three blown saves coming in a "break in case of emergency" situation, with the winning run already on base and one out in the eighth inning. Even then, he pitched well enough that the Padres still won after the save was blown.

Also Worth Considering: Jhoan Duran, Adrian Morejon, Tanner Scott, Didier Fuentes

AL Manager of the Year : Kevin Cash, Tampa Bay Rays

Chad Tracy gets a serious tip o' the cap for inheriting a mess from Alex Cora in late April and rallying the troops for a postseason berth.

However, Boston was supposed to be good and maybe needed that change of guard to eventually turn things around. Tampa Bay, on the other hand, was supposed to finish in dead last in the AL East, given a preseason win total of 76.5.

Thanks to Cash's leadership in the dugout, bets on the over cashed more than a month ago, as the Rays have already locked up the American League's No. 1 seed.

(If this award goes to Will Venable, though, no arguments here. Can't imagine there are many, if any, instances in history of a manager improving a team by at least 19 wins in back-to-back seasons, let alone in his first two years as a big-league manager.)

Also Worth Considering: Chad Tracy, Boston Red Sox; Will Venable, Chicago White Sox

NL Manager of the Year : Pat Murphy, Milwaukee Brewers

Like Tracy in Boston, three cheers to Don Mattingly in Philadelphia for taking over a 9-19 disaster in late April before steering the Phillies (barring a disaster scenario in this closing stretch) back to the postseason.

Mattingly merely got them back onto the right track, though, headed for a photo finish on that 89.5 preseason win total. Murphy should be headed for a third straight NL Manager of the Year award for repeatedly raising the bar in Milwaukee.

The Brewers set a franchise record with 97 wins last season. They've already reset that record this year.

Despite trading away three of last year's 10 most valuable players (Freddy Peralta, Caleb Durbin and Isaac Collins) during the winter.

Despite having last year's breakout pitcher, Quinn Priester, land on the IL in spring training and never return.

Despite losing Brandon Woodruff to a season-ending shoulder injury after just nine appearances.

And despite Christian Yelich dropping off a cliff for career-worst numbers.

Mattingly helped revive the Phillies, but Murphy might actually be a magician.

Also Worth Considering: Don Mattingly, Philadelphia Phillies

AL Platinum Glove : Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals

Witt also received this honor last season, when he was a tiny bit better and a good bit healthier.

Unless it's going to Dillon Dingler for proving that the art of framing pitches still matters in the ABS era, Witt ought to be the repeat winner of the American League's Platinum Glove.

It feels like a lifetime ago that he was a liability on defense as a rookie, but he has blossomed into one of the best five-tool players in the game today. He is sure to finish top seven in the AL MVP vote for a fourth straight year.

Also Worth Considering: Dillon Dingler, Detroit Tigers ; Ceddanne Rafaela, Boston Red Sox; Ezequiel Duran, Texas Rangers

NL Platinum Glove : Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs

The quest for a 40/40 season has drawn all the attention around PCA, but his range in center field might be even more ludicrous than what he is accomplishing on offense.

Per Statcast , he gets the best jump among qualified outfielders, and it's not even close.

As a result, he makes the improbable look routine and makes the impossible look anything but.

Crow-Armstrong has gone 8-for-16 on 5-star catch opportunities . He is the only qualified outfielder north of 30 percent (let alone 50 percent) in that category. He is also 12-for-15 on 4-star catch opportunities for a combined total of 20 catches and a 64.5 percent success rate on plays with a catch probability of 50 percent or lower. No other player has more than 13 such catches. AJ Ewing (6-for-7 on 4-star; 2-for-9 on 5-star; 50 percent total) is the only other with a success rate of 38 percent or better.

That's a lot of numbers to say that if anyone is going to replicate Willie Mays' iconic catch in the 1954 World Series, it's PCA. (He may well also homer and steal a bag while he's at it.)

Also Worth Considering: JJ Wetherholt, St. Louis Cardinals

Who Will Win : Kevin McGonigle, Detroit Tigers

Season Stats : .276/.376/.425, 17 HR, 70 RBI, 12 SB, 6.7 bWAR

It's wild to think McGonigle has been worth more wins above replacement than any other hitter in the American League, even though he hadn't made his Double-A debut until 15 months ago.

It's also wild to think Detroit couldn't even sniff the postseason in this year's American League while getting such a remarkable season from its 21-year-old infielder, but he certainly did everything in his power to keep the Tigers afloat.

At the moment, McGonigle has drawn 94 walks against 95 strikeouts. If he can get that ratio back up to 1.00 or better, he would become the first player to do so in an age-21-or-younger campaign with at least 400 plate appearances since Gary Sheffield in 1990.

Worthiest Challenger : Parker Messick, Cleveland Guardians

Season Stats : 183.1 IP, 12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 9.4 K/9, 6.2 bWAR

McGonigle might win in unanimous fashion, but Messick hasn't had an ERA north of 3.00 at any point in this entire season and really ought to be a more serious threat in this race. In starts in which Messick received at least three runs of support, Cleveland has gone 18-3. They might end up with a first-round bye because of it.

Deserved More Attention : Walbert Ureña, Los Angeles Angels

Who Will Win : Sal Stewart, Cincinnati Reds

Season Stats : .267/.335/.468, 32 HR, 110 RBI, 15 SB, 2.2 bWAR

Of the six races for major awards, NL ROY is the most debatable by far.

Whether you prefer Baseball-Reference or FanGraphs for your sabermetrics, JJ Wetherholt has Sal Stewart smoked in wins above replacement.

At a certain point, the RBI count matters more than the WAR calculation, as evidenced by the fact that all seven rookies to tally at least 111 RBI in a season over the past seven decades were named Rookie of the Year, four of them in unanimous fashion.

What's wild about Stewart sitting one shy of that plateau is that the Reds rank dead last in the National League in scoring. He has made the most of his opportunities, though, batting .301/.361/.569 with runners in scoring position. Because of that, there's a chance he's going to lead the majors in RBI.

Worthiest Challenger : JJ Wetherholt, St. Louis Cardinals

Season Stats : .240/.339/.365, 17 HR, 50 RBI, 14 SB, 4.6 bWAR

Wetherholt has had a preposterously impressive season in the field, last committing an error on April 10. Pete Crow-Armstrong will probably win the NL's Platinum Glove, but this rookie is the one player who could plausibly prevent that. Though a ton of his value added stems from his defense, the Cardinals aren't exactly hiding his bat in the lineup, batting him leadoff in every game that he has started.

Deserved More Attention : Logan Henderson, Milwaukee Brewers

Who Will Win : Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees

Season Stats : 190.2 IP, 14-6, 1.94 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 11.0 K/9, 7.0 bWAR

From 1972 to 2025, there were 12 cases of a pitcher recording at least 225 strikeouts with a sub-2.00 ERA and a sub-1.00 WHIP.

All 12 of them won the Cy Young Award. Cam Schlittler and Jacob Misiorowski will be joining that fraternity soon.

Schlittler has made 24 starts in which he allowed zero or one earned run and 24 starts in which he had at least as many strikeouts as the number of baserunners allowed.

The four-seamer is his moneymaker, responsible for more than half of his strikeouts. His sinker has been just as deadly. Opponents are hitting below .180 and slugging below .270 against both of those occasionally-more-than-100 MPH offerings.

Worthiest Challenger : Dylan Cease, Toronto Blue Jays

Season Stats : 169.0 IP, 11-6, 2.40 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 12.7 K/9, 5.6 bWAR

This was quite the two-horse race until about three weeks ago, when Cease's diminishing velocity started producing diminishing returns. Through the end of August, though, he was striking out 36.1 percent of opposing hitters, which is better than where Justin Verlander, Max Scherzer or Clayton Kershaw ever finished a season. For the Blue Jays' sake, here's hoping his shoulder inflammation doesn't turn into anything more long-lasting.

Deserved More Attention : Gavin Williams, Cleveland Guardians

Who Will Win : Jacob Misiorowski, Milwaukee Brewers

Season Stats : 169.1 IP, 15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 13.1 K/9, 6.1 bWAR

The Miz was to 2026 what Paul Skenes was to the 2024 and 2025 campaigns: appointment-viewing television every time he stepped on the mound.

The magnum opus was his 15-strikeout, one-hit shutout of the Phillies in mid-June. But his biggest "I beg your pardon, he's doing what now?" performance came against Colorado in late July, in which he struck out 12 of the first 13 batters he faced.

Unfortunately, that was his second start back after missing a bit of time with arm fatigue, so we all knew he wasn't going to pitch deep enough into the game to break the single-game strikeout record. Still, it was one of the most dominant abbreviated starts in recent memory and a sobering reminder of how untouchable Misiorowski can be when he's in his bag.

Worthiest Challenger : Cristopher Sánchez, Philadelphia Phillies

Season Stats : 200.0 IP, 18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 9.9 K/9, 7.7 bWAR

Atlanta's Chris Sale might actually finish second in this vote with his 2.18 ERA. However, while Atlanta pretty much always gave Sale at least five days' rest en route to just barely qualifying for the ERA title, Sánchez has been a workhorse, going at least 200 innings for the second straight year. Though May feels like ancient history at this point, that scoreless streak of 50.2 innings pitched was a legendary run.

Deserved More Attention : Jesús Luzardo, Philadelphia Phillies

Who Will Win : Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

Season Stats : .314/.431/.601, 41 HR, 102 RBI, 6.5 bWAR

If you want your MVP to be a five-tool guy, Alvarez isn't for you. He almost ranks dead last in the majors in baserunning run value, per Baseball Savant . While logging just 186.0 innings in left field—several pitchers have spent more time in the field than that—he committed multiple errors.

Also, if you want the MVP to be the best player on the best team, go ahead and scroll down a bit to Junior Caminero instead. Alvarez definitively has been Houston's most valuable player, but the Astros are a game below .500 and fighting to even reach the postseason.

With just five games left, though, Alvarez is the overwhelming favorite for AL MVP because he is leading the majors in batting average, on-base percentage and slugging percentage. No one has drawn more walks. Only Pete Crow-Armstrong has more total bases.

If he ends up one home run or one RBI shy of the Triple Crown, maybe we can retroactively award him a solo shot for that "foul ball" that he hammered off the rafters on Opening Day?

Worthiest Challenger : Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays

Season Stats : .275/.361/.525, 41 HR, 97 RBI, 5.7 bWAR

In case you thought Caminero's 45-homer campaign last year was a "benefited from playing home games at a spring training venue" fluke, he doubled down with an even more impressive run through 2026. Not quite as many home runs, but he did join 1953-54 Eddie Mathews as the only hitters in MLB history with multiple seasons of 40+ home runs by the end of their age-22 season. Caminero also improved his on-base percentage by 50 points, becoming more of an overall asset at the dish.

Deserved More Attention : Miguel Vargas, Chicago White Sox

Who Will Win : Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs

Season Stats : .282/.373/.579, 45 HR, 107 RBI, 39 SB, 9.8 bWAR

What's bonkers about Crow-Armstrong now running away with the NL MVP and one swipe away from the 40/40 club is that it seemed impossible four months ago.

In late May, most of the discourse about PCA involved a couple of careless errors in center field, his disappointing sub-.700 OPS or that profane altercation with a White Sox fan. Through 58 games, he was hitting .224 with six home runs and 12 stolen bases. Trea Turner (.222, seven and 11, respectively) was in pretty much the exact same boat. We're still waiting on him to snap out of his funk.

Since May 30, though, Crow-Armstrong has triple-slashed .312/.404/.693 while operating at 162-game paces of 64 home runs and 44 stolen bases.

Even if Shohei Ohtani hadn't gotten hurt, PCA's run to a possible 10 WAR season probably would've been enough to win this vote.

Worthiest Challenger : Shohei Ohtani, Los Angeles Dodgers

Season Stats : .277/.380/.522, 30 HR, 80 RBI, 11 SB; 85.2 IP, 1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 10.0 K/9, 6.5 bWAR

Ohtani is one of three hitters with at least 30 home runs and an OPS of .900 or better. The others are inevitable MVPs Alvarez and PCA. Ohtani is also one of three pitchers with at least 80 innings, a sub-2.00 ERA and a sub-1.00 WHIP. The others are inevitable Cy Youngs Schlittler and Misiorowski. He hasn't pitched since early July and hasn't been the same hitter since early August. But if you've been disappointed by Ohtani's season, you might want to recalibrate.

Deserved More Attention : Elly De La Cruz, Cincinnati Reds

articles.title: ‘Definitely Something to Build on,’ Bryan Reynolds Gives Thoughts on Pirates Season
articles.summary: PITTSBURGH – Bryan Reynolds, the Pirates’ longest-tenured player, has accomplished a lot in his eight-year MLB career. The 31-year-old has […]
articles.body:
PITTSBURGH – Bryan Reynolds , the Pirates' longest-tenured player, has accomplished a lot in his eight-year MLB career.

The 31-year-old has been an All-Star twice. He finished fourth in the 2019 National League Rookie of the Year race and received MVP votes in 2021. When he signed a $106.75 million extension in 2023, it was a franchise record.

This year, Reynolds could add a couple more individual achievements to his resume. The switch-hitter notched his 40th double of the season in Tuesday's win over the Cardinals at PNC Park. Reynolds is the first Pirate to hit the mark since Nate McLouth had 46 in 2007, and he's only the second switch-hitter in franchise history to have a 40-double season, joining Bobby Bonilla (44, 1991).

Reynolds leads MLB in the category as the only player so far to hit the benchmark.

"It was cool. I hit it and I told myself I was going to second no matter what. Luckily the throw was off," Reynolds said of eighth-inning double off Cade Winquest. "Doubles are cool, so it's good to hit a lot of those. It would've been nice to sprinkle in some home runs too, but I'll take the 40 doubles."

Part of the reason Reynolds was able to record 40 doubles this season is because of how available he's been. He's appeared in every game the team has had this season and is looking to become the first Pirate to play all 162 games since Jason Bay in 2005.

"I think that's pretty cool, being available," he explained. "I haven't started every game but getting into every game, I've wanted to do that in my career. I've had some hiccups the last few years, but hopefully this will be the year."

While Reynolds' individual performance is on par with what he's done throughout his career, the team success the Pirates have had has been unlike what he's experienced.

Although the Pirates missed out on the playoffs, they are on the verge of their first winning season since 2018 — the year before Reynolds made his MLB debut.

"I think throughout the year, there was an expectation that coming to the field, you have a real good chance to win, which hasn't really been the case in some years past," he explained. "Yeah, I think to be where we're at — obviously it's not where we'd like to be — but a few games over .500 with a couple games left and we weren't at full strength for really any of the year, except for maybe three weeks total. Just continuing to fight."

The Pirates were without regulars such as Oneil Cruz , Konnor Griffin, Ryan O'Hearn and Spencer Horwitz due to lengthy IL stints. Had they not had to deal with major injury blows, Reynolds feels the Pirates would be even better than they are now.

"It's tough when you take good bats out of the lineup," he said. "Guys stepped up, too, but it's just a lot for the lineup to carry for an extended time. We were just kind of unlucky with that. We've got everybody back right now and we've been really good. It just stinks that it could have been much of the season like that."

After a 5-1 loss to the Cardinals on Wednesday, the Pirates are 80-78 and two wins away from clinching just their fifth winning in the last 34 years. It's not where the Pirates wanted their season to end, but it shows some progress.

"Definitely gives you confidence," Reynolds said of a winning season and strong finish carrying over into next year. "This last September or whatever, we've got a good record, and that's pretty much at full strength. Gives us some confidence to show us that we're capable of it. Obviously, we didn't do the ultimate goal, but a few steps in the right direction."

It's largely been lip service to say the Pirates are heading into next year with a real chance to compete. But heading into 2027, the team feels a strong foundation is set to help them finally get over the hump.

"It's the best year I've had here, so definitely something to build on," Reynolds said of the team's success.

articles.title: 2026 MLB Free Agents Predictions for Top Pitchers Set to Hit Open Market
articles.summary: With the threat of a lockout looming over all things MLB, there's no telling how this year's free agency will play out.
articles.body:
With the threat of a lockout looming over all things MLB, there's no telling how this year's free agency will play out.

What is certain, though, is that the market will feature difference-making pitchers. Or maybe one full-fledged difference-maker and then a slew of rock-solid starters capable of beefing up just about any rotation.

This is the Tarik Skubal offseason with the two-time Cy Young standing head, shoulders and a full body underneath above the rest of the free agent pool. While he'll be the biggest star, he is far from the only hurler capable of attracting significant interest on the hot stove.

Let's peak ahead, then, and guesstimate what the future holds for three of the top pitchers in free agency.

As far as contract years go, Peralta's will be remembered as a massive disappointment. His trade to the New York Mets—seemingly the first step ahead of a long partnership—proved a horrendous fit, as the 2025 All-Star labored his way to a 4.99 ERA across 22 starts before being mercifully moved to Tampa Bay at the deadline.

To the surprise of perhaps no one, the Rays found ways of getting Peralta back on track. While not as dominant as last season, his nine-start stretch with the team so far has featured a reasonable 3.60 ERA and a 0.980 WHIP. That's a better ERA than his career mark and a lower WHIP than he had in 2025.

His strikeouts remain lower than ever, but fortunately the same holds true for his walks. And considering he had 200-plus punchouts each of the previous three seasons, perhaps suitors will simply see this year as anomaly and be willing to bet on a further return to form.

He still might have to settle for a short-term prove-it pact before getting the kind of long-term deal he desires, which might helps the Rays' hopes of retaining him. Then again, if someone opts to pay him for what his long-term track record says he's worth, that might bump him out of Tampa's price range.

Prediction: Peralta signs a two-year deal with the San Diego Padres.

Rogers has one of the more interesting stat pages you'll find, as it features a couple dominant campaigns, a couple clunkers and some so-so efforts sprinkled in, too. That won't make him the easiest open-market evaluation, but it would help if would-be suitors focused on his 2025 effort (1.81 ERA across 109.2 innings) and his more recent 2026 performances.

Things were plenty messy earlier this season, but they've been mostly calm of late. Since the start of June, he has pieced together a 2.92 ERA over 117 innings with 115 strikeouts against 21 walks.

His inconsistency will work against him, but the fact he'll only turn 29 in November might counteract that and then some. Long-term pacts with non-ace pitchers are always dicey, but there are reasons to believe he could be solid or better for most (if not all) of a four- or five-year deal.

That doesn't mean he'll for sure fetch one, obviously, but given his up-and-down numbers, it's easy to imagine he wouldn't mind locking into a longer contract if the salary figure is right. Nine figures could be a realistic target.

Prediction: Rogers signs a four-year deal with the Toronto Blue Jays.

Free agency isn't necessarily arriving at the ideal time for Skubal, as he hasn't been quite as razor-sharp this season as he was over the last two (both Cy Young award-winners). On a related note, he also had to navigate around an elbow procedure and a midseason move from Detroit to L.A., so all things considered, it's still been a pretty awesome campaign.

Which makes sense since he is—objectively speaking—a pretty awesome pitcher. You have to go all the way back to 2022 to find the last time his ERA landed north of 3.00. During the three-plus seasons since, he's had a 2.50 ERA over 619.1 innings with 10.9 K/9 against 1.6 BB/9.

A healthy Skubal might be the best and most dominant pitcher in the Majors. Even in this uncertain financial climate, he could fetch north of $400 million in total contract value. If he winds up with a shorter deal, his average annual salary could bypass the $43.33 million record shared by Justin Verlander and Max Scherzer.

All deep-pocketed clubs will likely want to be in on the bidding, including his deep-pocketed current employer. Dark-horse options could emerge, too, especially if he's amenable to shorter deals with bigger salaries. The New York Mets could and should make this interesting, but the Dodgers could absolutely win another Skubal sweepstakes.

Prediction: Skubal signs a 10-year deal and stays in L.A.

articles.title: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. Defends Viral Quote on $500M Blue Jays Contract, 'I'm Not Lying'
articles.summary: As the Toronto Blue Jays put the finishing touches on a disappointing 2026 season, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. isn't backing down from a recent quote he about his individual performance and the contract extension he signed last year.
articles.body:
As the Toronto Blue Jays put the finishing touches on a disappointing 2026 season, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. isn't backing down from a recent quote he about his individual performance and the contract extension he signed last year.

In a Spanish-language interview with Veronica Batista (h/t Mike Wilner of the Toronto Star ) that published Wednesday, Guerrero said his contract "wasn't for what I'm going to do" but "for what I already did."

After those comments received criticism from fans, Guerrero told reporters , via interpreter Hector Lebron, later that same day "I'm not lying" when asked if he regretted that assessment.

Guerrero went on to explain he's not happy with how he has played this season, but in his "personal opinion" players are getting paid for their past output rather than future performance:

"That was a quote from the interview when she asked me how I felt about this year. I said that, obviously, I feel really bad about the year that I had, that I couldn't help my team get to the postseason. I said I felt — that it's my personal opinion — that every player gets paid for what they have done. With that said, you guys have got to remember that I signed my contract at the beginning of last year, then I did put up a good year. Then the kind of playoffs that I had to help the team get into the World Series."

Guerrero signed a 14-year, $500 million extension with the Blue Jays in April 2025. It was the start of what turned out to be a magical year for both parties, as Guerrero helped Toronto win the AL East and make a run to Game 7 of the World Series before losing to the Los Angeles Dodgers.

This season has been arguably the worst of Guerrero's career. He is hitting .263/.335/.360 with nine homers in 142 games. The Blue Jays were officially eliminated from playoff contention on Wednesday, making the release of his interview and the comment even worse.

It's not inaccurate to say teams pay players based on what they have done because it informs their analysis of what they will do in the future. On a contract the length and size Guerrero signed, there will usually be some overpay on the back end but the hope is the overall value nets out on the positive side.

No one was expecting that 2026, the first year in which the deal kicked in, would be part of the downside for Guerrero. He is only 27 and there should be a bounce back next season.

It's perhaps worth pointing out the last time Guerrero was worth fewer than 2.0 fWAR in a season was 2023. He came back the following year with arguably his best season, posting a .323/.396/.544 slash line and 5.2 fWAR in 159 games.

Inconsistency has been a hallmark of Guerrero's entire career. In the eight full seasons he has played since debuting in 2019, he has been worth 1.2 fWAR or fewer four times and at least 3.3 fWAR four times.

There might not be a safer bet in 2027 than Guerrero returning to All-Star form.

articles.title: Yankees' Ben Rice Hyped as 'One of the Best' By Aaron Judge After 41st HR of 2026 MLB Season
articles.summary: New York Yankees superstar outfielder heaped praise on first baseman Ben Rice after he slugged his 40th and 41st home runs of the season on Wednesday.
articles.body:
New York Yankees superstar outfielder heaped praise on first baseman Ben Rice after he slugged his 40th and 41st home runs of the season on Wednesday.

Speaking to reporters after Rice's dominant performance in the Yanks' 9-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays, Judge said, "One thing I always tell guys, the difference between minor leaguers and big leaguers is the consistency. He's one of the best. I can look up at the clock and I know exactly where he's going to be in the cage. You know what he's doing in the training room, the weight room. It's just every single day, man. This guy's a machine."

Judge missed a large portion of this season with a fractured rib, and he went back on the injured list last week due to a calf strain.

While Judge has long been the centerpiece of the Yankees' lineup, Rice has taken up that mantle for much of the 2026 campaign.

Playing in only his second full MLB season, the 27-year-old Rice owns new career highs across the board, slashing .263/.362/.537 with 41 homers, 97 RBI and 103 runs scored.

The power-hitting lefty leads the Yankees in home runs, RBI, runs, walks, on-base percentage and slugging percentage among qualified players.

Despite falling short of the American League East crown due to the strong play of the Rays this season, the Yankees are still considered one of the teams to beat in the AL come playoff time.

With Judge's status for the postseason up in the air, it could largely be up to Rice to lead the way offensively, at least in the early going of the playoffs.

Potentially not having a player of Judge's caliber would sink most teams, but Rice ensures that the Yankees still have a dangerous lineup to go along with one of the best starting rotations in baseball.

articles.title: Aaron Judge Calls Out Yankees' Aaron Boone For Comments on Injury, Status for 2026 MLB Playoffs
articles.summary: New York Yankees star Aaron Judge has questioned manager Aaron Boone publicly discussing his potential availability for the American League wild-card series as he recovers from a calf injury.
articles.body:
New York Yankees star Aaron Judge has questioned manager Aaron Boone publicly discussing his potential availability for the American League wild-card series as he recovers from a calf injury.

After the Yankees' win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday, Judge seemed unhappy that Boone described his injury as a "moderate" calf strain.

"I don't know why he used those words," Judge told reporters when asked about the situation.

Boone made his comment on Tuesday when he also said the Yankees are "planning on him not being a part of that" after being asked about Judge's availability for the wild-card round, but they aren't ruling him out at this point.

The Yankees skipper also said Judge received an injection in his calf on Monday.

Judge said Wednesday his "goal" is to return as soon as possible, though he didn't offer any timetable:

"My goal is to come back as soon as I can. That's what we're doing right now. If he says I'm not going to be ready, I've got no control over that. I got control over what I can do to try to get back as soon as I can. If you ask me if I'm gonna be back, I'm gonna tell you, I'm doing everything I can every single day I show up here to get back and be ready to go."

Judge returned to the lineup on Sept. 8 after missing 85 games due to a stress fracture in his rib. The three-time AL MVP made seven starts before leaving a Sept. 16 game against the Minnesota Twins early due to a calf injury.

The Yankees placed Judged on the 10-day IL on Sept. 19 after an MRI revealed a calf strain. They did not say the severity of the strain or when he might be able to return.

New York is locked in as the No. 4 seed in the AL playoffs and will host the Boston Red Sox in the best-of-three wild card series starting on Sept. 29. Judge is eligible to be activated off the IL on Sunday, the final day of the regular season.

Judge hit just .174/.208/.304 with one homer and 13 strikeouts in 24 plate appearances in the seven games after returning from his rib injury. He is hitting .241/.360/.511 with 18 homers in 66 games overall this season.

articles.title: Identical twin brothers team up to umpire their first MLB doubleheader
articles.summary: Tyler Jones umpired the first game of this week’s Blue Jays-Orioles series, then was napping the next day.
articles.body: BALTIMORE — Tyler Jones umpired the first game of this week’s Blue Jays-Orioles series, then was napping the next day. His brother Austin called and told him the middle game of the series was rained out. A doubleheader Wednesday meant Austin — who, in addition to being Tyler’s identical twin, is also an umpire — was on his way to Baltimore to work the games alongside his brother. “This is something we’ve dreamed about forever,” Tyler Jones said. “We were told last year, ‘OK, if we can make it happen, we’ll make it happen.’ And it didn’t. The schedules didn’t align. Even this year we weren’t even sure if it was going to happen or not, and then it was kind of a shock.” The 31-year-old twins called both ends of Wednesday’s doubleheader, each won by Baltimore by a 4-2 score. Austin worked first base in the opener and Tyler was at second. Then they swapped for the nightcap — although the numbers on their uniforms were the only easy way to tell them apart. The two are on a list of Triple-A call-up umpires who fill in at the big league level for injuries, illnesses, vacations and other reasons of absence. There are typically five umpires on a crew for a doubleheader instead of four, so Austin Jones was added. Austin umpired his first major league game in 2024, Tyler in 2025. They’d worked a game together in the Gulf Coast League and the Arizona Fall League, but never in the majors. “We talk to each other daily, especially about baseball and about everything, what we go through on a day-to-day basis,” Tyler Jones said. “But to be able to live it together, and come to the ballpark and see him in the locker room and play cards with him before the game and share that experience was probably the best part.” The Jones twins have joined a small group of umpiring families in big league history. There have been fathers and sons, such as Harry and Hunter Wendelstedt, and brothers, such as John and Mark Hirschbeck. Tyler Jones jokes that he got into umpiring because “I was a really bad baseball player.” They certainly started young, working youth games and earning some money when they were in high school. “Baseball was what we ate, slept or thought of every single moment of the day,” Austin Jones said. “But it was to the point, I guess, after umpire school. We did umpire school together, and we roomed together. We had never really lived on our own, we were 18 years old. So it was our first time out of the house, doing things on our own, and we said, ‘Man, if this is kind of what life in professional baseball is like, this is pretty cool.’” The Jones brothers had their parents, wives and Austin’s kids at the games Wednesday. “It was cool to look over, and that’s something my wife told me,” Austin said. “She was like, ‘Hey, when you’re out there, obviously you’re looking at your partners every pitch every play, but take a second and look at him not as just the guy working first base, your partner. Look at him as your brother.’ So I did that a little bit moreso tonight, the second game.”

images.caption: Second base umpire Tyler Jones, left, and his twin brother first base umpire Austin Jones talk before the first baseball game of a doubleheader between the Baltimore Orioles and the Toronto Blue Jays, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026, in Baltimore.

articles.title: Latest MLB Playoff Picture 2026, World Series Bracket and Wild Card Race
articles.summary: The undecideds in the MLB playoff race remained undecided on Wednesday night.
articles.body:
The undecideds in the MLB playoff race remained undecided on Wednesday night.

Five teams had a shot at securing their postseason tickets, but all of them came up short. So, they'll be left waiting at least one more day to snag a seat at the table.

Some feel inevitable, but others are way too close to call. The AL West, for instance, has a tie between the Texas Rangers and Houston Astros for now, but the latter holds the spot by way of a tiebreaker. In the AL Central, the Cleveland Guardians have just a one-game cushion on the resurgent Chicago White Sox.

All of this will get settled over the next few days, but let's look at all of the pertinent races snapshot-style before examining Thursday's clinching scenarios.

*x-clinched division; y-clinched wild card; e-eliminated from playoff contention

It'll be an especially busy Thursday night in the MLB world, and the many clinching scenarios at play can attest to that.

Over in the AL, the Guardians and White Sox both have chances to clinch playoff berths. For Cleveland, it can happen by way of a win over Boston, a Texas loss to the Mets or a Houston loss to the A's. For Chicago, a win over Kansas City or a Texas loss to the Mets would get it done.

The Red Sox have their own stakes at play, since they'd lock in the second wild card spot with a win over the Guardians or a White Sox loss to the Royals. Boston will have All-Star Ranger Suárez on the bump, while Cleveland has rookie Daniel Espino as an opener and southpaw Joey Cantillo working in bulk behind him.

Over in the NL, the top two playoff seeds and three different playoff berths could be claimed before the night is finished.

The Brewers can lock up the No. 1 seed with a win over the Phillies and a Dodgers' loss to the Padres. The Dodgers, meanwhile, could ensure they'll finish no worse than No. 2 with either a win over the Padres or a Braves loss to the Reds.

The Cubs, Padres and Phillies could all clinch playoff berths if the Diamondbacks lose to the Rockies. Should Arizona take care of business, then Chicago would get in with a win over Miami, San Diego would clinch with a win over L.A. and Philadelphia would secure a berth with a win over Milwaukee.
